title: On Gratitude, and the Richly Woven Tapestry of 'School'
author: Birmingham Teacher
summary: Writing as Open Evening season begins, a Birmingham secondary head reflects on what a school owes the families who choose it. She grounds her long-standing advocacy for a knowledge-rich curriculum in her own upbringing at a 1990s comprehensive in north Birmingham, arguing that rigorous, high-expectation schooling functioned as a genuine social leveller regardless of family income or postcode. Now leading a school where more than 70% of pupils receive the Pupil Premium, she treats equitable access to a demanding education as an urgent, present-tense moral duty rather than an abstract policy aim. The heart of the piece is a long, itemized list of specific things she is grateful to her own school for — learning the clarinet, debating, GCSE Latin, an orchestra trip, a school exchange to Germany, a classical tour of Greece — offered as evidence of what a genuinely rich school experience looks like beyond exam grades. She is candid that her own school still has work to do, framing the essay as much as a challenge to herself as a tribute to her alma mater. Throughout, she resists collapsing school quality into attainment data alone, insisting that culture, enrichment, and relationships are inseparable from real equity of opportunity.
points: Argues a knowledge-rich curriculum was the 'great leveller' of her own working-class schooling, not exam grades alone.
Frames closing opportunity gaps as an urgent, present-tense duty rather than a long-term goal, given her school's 70%+ Pupil Premium population.

Uses a detailed personal inventory — debate, GCSE Latin, orchestra, a Germany exchange, a classical tour of Greece — to define school quality as encompassing culture and enrichment, not just academics.
Credits her own school with sky-high expectations that did not vary by family income or neighborhood.
quotes: My school was a great leveller; it was equity embodied. It didn’t matter if your parents were well-off or not, if you lived in leafy suburbia or, like me, in an area rife with crime and bullied by poverty.
I don’t want kids to have to be lucky. I don’t want children’s futures determined by the toss of a coin or the roll of a dice. Their futures are here, now, and urgent.
As the principal of a school with now more than 70% of our pupils in receipt of the Pupil Premium, I feel this keenly. It is a weighty responsibility.

And getting it right is about helping children make progress and doing well academically. It’s also about many other things, laced together in a complex, embroidered, richly woven tapestry of how glorious school can be.
I truly believe that getting a grade 4 or 5 or above in English and mathematics is the gateway to a world of possibilities for children. It flings open doors that would otherwise be tightly shut.

For flying me to Germany with my peers in Year 9 on an exchange to stay with a lovely family. For arranging for me to go even though we didn’t have enough room in our house for my exchange partner to come and stay with us in Birmingham.
For the classical tour of Greece when I was in Year 12. For the Parthenon, for Delphi, and for Epidaurus.
